links.note: 1054 says that asking (இரத்தலும்) of those who do not know concealment even in a dream is 'like giving' (ஈதலே போலும்). 1061 takes exactly those givers, who give gladly without hiding (கரவாது உவந்தீயும்), and says that even with them (கண்ணும்) not asking is worth a crore more (இரவாமை கோடி உறும்). The best case that chapter 106 allows is the case 1061 ranks below not asking at all.

1035 says those who eat by the work of their hands (கைசெய்தூண் மாலையவர்) do not beg (இரவார்) and give to askers without concealing (கரவாது ஈவர்). 1061 praises not asking (இரவாமை) even from givers who do not conceal (கரவாது ஈயும்). Read together, the unconcealing giver and the one who does not ask are the same person in 1035, which shows how the higher course of 1061 is actually lived.

1058 says that without askers (இரப்பாரை இல்லாயின்) the wide world would move like a wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந் தற்று); Parimelazhagar takes this as showing the world needs askers. 1062 says that if living by begging is required (இரந்தும் உயிர்வாழ்தல் வேண்டின்), the maker of the world should himself wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக உலகியற்றியான்). The conflict holds if 1058 is read as approving a world that contains beggars; 1062 treats such an arrangement as grounds for a curse.

377 says even those who heap up crores can enjoy them only in the way the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை). 1062 addresses the same figure as the maker of the world (உலகியற்றியான்) and curses him if what he has laid down includes living by begging; Parimelazhagar explains that he assigns each life its livelihood. 377 states the allotment as a fact, and 1062 judges the one who allots.

1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealment, all the afflictions of want perish together (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). 1063 says nothing is harder than the hardness of saying 'we will end the affliction of poverty by begging' (இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம்). They conflict if 1063 is read, as Manakkudavar reads it, to mean begging does not end poverty; Parimelazhagar instead faults the choice of begging over effort.

616 says effort makes fortune and lack of effort brings want in (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்); Parimelazhagar applies it to kings. 1063 calls it hardness (வன்மை) to think poverty's affliction can be ended by begging, and Parimelazhagar explains that the proper path, effort, is being set aside. 1063 applies 616's rule to the poor man and names begging as the wrong substitute for effort.

1063 calls hard the thought that poverty can be ended by begging (இரந்து தீர்வாம்). 1068 gives a picture of why: begging is a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits when it strikes the rock of concealment (கரவென்னும் பார்). Manakkudavar says 1068 states the cause of poverty not ending, which makes it the reason behind 1063's claim.

988 says poverty is no disgrace to a person if he has the firmness called worth (சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 1064 says the worth (சால்பு) that will not consent to asking even when there are no means (இடமில்லாக் காலும் இரவொல்லா) is too great for all space to hold. 1064 shows one thing the firmness of 988 consists in: poverty does not disgrace the worthy because they do not turn it into begging.

218 says those who see their duty do not slacken in ஒப்புரவு even in a season without means (இடனில் பருவத்தும்). 1064 says worth does not consent to asking even at a time without means (இடமில்லாக் காலும்). The same test, what a person does when resources are gone, is applied to giving in 218 and to asking in 1064: the good neither stop giving nor start begging.

64 says the gruel (கூழ்) stirred by one's children's small hands is far sweeter than amrita (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிதே). 1065 says nothing is sweeter (இனியது இல்) than eating what one's own effort brought (தாள் தந்தது), though it is gruel thin as clear water (தெண்ணீர் அடுபுற்கை); Parimelazhagar adds that it equals amrita. In both, plain gruel is made sweet by whose hands are behind it, the children's in 64 and one's own labour in 1065.

1033 says only those who plough and eat (உழுதுண்டு) truly live, and all others bow and eat and walk behind (தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல்பவர்). 1065 says nothing is sweeter than eating what one's own effort gave (தாள் தந்தது உண்ணல்), however thin. Both rank food by how it was got: 1033 in terms of standing and dependence, 1065 in terms of taste.

In 1107 the man says the woman's embrace is like living in one's own home and eating one's own food after sharing it (தம்மில் இருந்து தமது பாத்து உண்டற்று); Parimelazhagar glosses 'one's own' as wealth that came by one's own effort. 1065 says nothing is sweeter than eating what one's effort gave. The lover uses as his standard of pleasure the very thing 1065 states as a rule, though his is a speech in the Book of Love and not a teaching.

222 says taking is bad even if it is called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). 1066 says that even if one asks for water for a cow (ஆவிற்கு நீரென்று இரப்பினும்), nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both take the cow as a case of asking for the sake of virtue. Both verses deny that a good purpose removes what is wrong with asking or receiving.

656 says that even if one must see one's own mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசி காண்பான் ஆயினும்), one should not do what the worthy condemn. 1066 says that even asking water for a cow is degrading to the tongue (நாவிற்கு இளிவந்தது). Each picks the most sympathetic motive available, a hungry mother or a thirsty cow, and holds that it does not excuse the act.

1053 says that even asking, standing before those of unconcealing heart who know their duty, has a certain beauty (இரப்பும் ஓர் ஏஎர் உடைத்து). 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking (இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்), even for a cow's water. They conflict if 1066 is read as covering every act of asking; on a narrower reading 1053 speaks only of asking from the right giver, which 1066 does not mention.

1051 says to ask if you find those fit to be asked, and if they conceal the blame is theirs and not yours (அவர்பழி தம்பழி அன்று). 1067 has the poet himself beg of all who beg (இரப்பன் இரப்பாரை எல்லாம்) not to ask of those who conceal (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). 1051 clears the refused asker of blame; 1067 adds that being blameless is not enough reason to ask a concealer, and Parimelazhagar says it forbids the asking that costs one's honour.

1067 asks beggars not to beg of those who conceal (கரப்பார்). 1077 describes such people from the other side: the base will not even shake a wet hand (ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார்) for anyone but those whose fist would break their jaw. 1077 shows what asking a concealer comes to, and why 1067 pleads against it.

1068 calls asking a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits on the rock of concealment; the commentators supply poverty as the sea it was meant to cross. In 1164 the woman says the sea of love exists but the safe raft to swim it (ஏமப் புணை) does not. Both use the figure of a sea that must be crossed and a vessel that fails, 1068 as a teaching about begging and 1164 as a lover's complaint.

306 says anger burns even the safe raft called one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப் புணை). 1068 calls asking a boat without safety (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that breaks on concealment. The same word for safety (ஏமம், ஏமாப்பு) marks the vessel in both: one's people are the safe one in 306, and asking is named the unsafe one in 1068.

1057 says that on seeing those who give without scorn, the heart rejoices deep within (உள்ளம் உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து). 1069 says that at the thought of asking the heart melts (உள்ளம் உருகும்), and at the thought of concealment even what remains is gone (உள்ளதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்). Both follow the heart (உள்ளம்) through the act of asking; 1057 gives its state before a good giver and 1069 its state before a refusal. Parimelazhagar takes the heart in 1069 as the speaker's, while he reports others take it as the asker's.

224 says being asked is unpleasant (இன்னாது இரக்கப் படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face. 1069 says the heart melts at the thought of asking. Taken together they say asking is painful on both sides, for the one asked in 224 and for the one who asks or contemplates it in 1069, and that only the gift ends the pain.

230 says nothing is more bitter than dying, yet even dying is sweet when giving is not possible (ஈதல் இயையாக் கடை). 1070 says the asker's life goes at the word of refusal (சொல்லாடப் போஒம் உயிர்) and asks where the concealer's life hides (யாங்கொளிக்கும் கொல்லோ). 230 gives the giver's view that life without giving is not worth keeping; 1070 puts that standard to the one who can give and refuses, and wonders that his life stays.

223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை), and giving, are found in one of good family; Pope takes the words as the giver's excuse, while Parimelazhagar first takes them as the asker's plea. 1070 says the asker's life leaves when the word is spoken (சொல்லாட); Parimelazhagar takes this as the concealer saying 'no'. On Pope's reading of 223 both verses are about the word of refusal, which the well-born never say and which 1070 says kills the hearer.

993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people (உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்று), and that fitting likeness is likeness of character (பண்பொத்தல்). 1071 says the base are just like people (மக்களே போல்வர்) and that no such resemblance has been seen elsewhere. 993 gives the rule and 1071 the case: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both explain that the base match people in form and not in qualities.

600 says those without inner drive are trees, and their being human in form is the only difference (மரம் மக்களாதலே வேறு). 1071 says the base resemble people exactly (மக்களே போல்வர்). Both treat the human shape as something that can be present without what makes a person, lacking drive in 600 and lacking character in 1071.

201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear, and the excellent do fear, the intoxication called evil deed (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்). 1072 says the base are more fortunate than those who know what is good, because they have no distress in the heart (நெஞ்சத்து அவலம் இலர்). 1072 puts 201's fact in mock praise: Parimelazhagar says the verse scorns by implication, and that the point is their not fearing blame.

839 says the friendship of fools is very sweet (பெரிதினிது), because parting from it gives no pain. 1072 says the base are fortunate (திருவுடையர்), because their hearts have no distress. Both verses praise a bad thing for the absence of a pain that only something of value would cause.

1073 says the base are like the gods because they too act as they please (மேவன செய்தொழுகலான்). 1075 says that where the base show proper conduct (ஆசாரம்) it is fear, and beyond that a little if there is something they desire. 1075 marks the limit on 1073's freedom: their doing as they please stops only at fear or gain; Parimelazhagar says doing what they like is their nature and conduct is not.

1072 calls the base fortunate (திருவுடையர்) for having no distress of heart, and 1073 calls them like the gods (தேவர் அனையர்) for doing as they please. Both give praise that is meant as blame; Parimelazhagar says so of each. The two together describe one condition, no inner check in 1072 and no outer one in 1073.

978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself in admiration of itself (சிறுமை அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). 1074 says the base man, on seeing those worse than himself, outdoes them and swaggers (மிகப்பட்டுச் செம்மாக்கும்); this follows Parimelazhagar's reading of அகப்பட்டி as those of looser conduct, while Manakkudavar reads the word quite differently. On Parimelazhagar's reading 1074 shows where the self-admiration of 978 finds its material: in comparison with someone lower.

1016 says the high do not care for the wide world unless they have shame as their fence (நாண்வேலி). 1075 says the conduct of the base is fear (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம்), which Parimelazhagar takes as fear of harm from the king. Each verse names what keeps a kind of person within bounds: shame from inside for the high, fear from outside for the base.

201 says those given to evil deeds do not fear (தீவினையார் அஞ்சார்) the intoxication of evil deed. 1075 says fear is the whole of the base man's good conduct (அச்சமே). The two are consistent once the object of fear is separated: 201 means fear of the evil deed itself, and 1075, on Parimelazhagar's reading, fear of punishment.

1075 says the base behave properly out of fear. 1078 says the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed (கொல்லப் பயன்படும் கீழ்). 1078 applies the rule of 1075 to giving: what fear does for their conduct, force does for their generosity.

1076 says the base are like a beaten drum (அறைபறை அன்னர்) because they carry a secret they heard (கேட்ட மறை) to others. In 1180 the woman says the town easily gets the secret (மறை) in the heart of those like her whose eyes are beaten drums (அறைபறை கண்ணார்). The same pair of words, drum and secret, is used for a fault of character in 1076 and for a lover's eyes that give her away against her will in 1180.

221 says giving to those who have nothing is what giving is (வறியார்க்கொன்று ஈவதே ஈகை), and all other giving has the nature of a loan to be returned. 1077 says the base will not even shake a wet hand (ஈர்ங்கை விதிரார்) except for those whose bent fist would break their jaw; Parimelazhagar sums up that they give nothing to the weak and everything to those who hurt them. The base man's giving in 1077 is the reverse of 221's definition: it goes only to the strong.

1077 says the base give only to those who would break their jaw. 1078 states the same with a contrast and a figure: the worthy are of use at a word (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர்), and the base, like sugar-cane, when crushed (கொல்லப் பயன்படும்). Parimelazhagar treats the two verses as a pair on how the base give.

1078 says the worthy are of use as soon as they are told (சொல்லப் பயன்படுவர் சான்றோர்). 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, belong to one of good family; Parimelazhagar records a second reading on which the giver gives before the asker has to say it. On that reading 223 goes one step beyond 1078: the worthy of 1078 give at a word, and the well-born of 223 give before the word.

216 says wealth with a person of நயன் is like a fruit-bearing tree ripening in the middle of the town (பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று). 1078 says the base are like sugar-cane (கரும்புபோல்), of use only when crushed. Both use a plant's yield (பயன்) as the figure for how a person's wealth reaches others: the tree offers its fruit in the open, and the cane gives nothing until it is pressed.

166 says the kin of one who envies a gift will perish with nothing to wear or eat (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்). 1079 says the base man, on seeing others clothed and fed (உடுப்பதூஉம் உண்பதூஉம் காணின்), is able to find a fault in them. The same phrase for clothing and food names what the envious man cannot bear to see in 1079 and what envy costs his own house in 166.

980 says greatness hides another's weak point and smallness only tells faults (சிறுமைதான் குற்றமே கூறிவிடும்). 1079 says the base man is able to see a blemish in others (பிறர்மேல் வடுக்காண வற்றாகும்) when he sees them clothed and fed. 1079 adds the motive that 980 leaves out: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both take it as envy of others' prosperity, and Parimelazhagar adds that the fault may be invented.

220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth buying even by selling oneself (விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது). 1080 says the base are fit only to sell themselves quickly (விற்றற்கு உரியர் விரைந்து) when something befalls them. Selling oneself appears in both: as the price a good person would pay to keep helping others in 220, and as the base man's first move to get out of trouble in 1080.

969 says those like the yak that will not live once its hair is lost give up life when honour is at stake (உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்). 1080 says the base, when something befalls them (ஒன்று உற்றக்கால்), hurry to sell themselves. The two verses give opposite answers to the same moment of pressure: the honourable give up life to keep themselves, and the base give up themselves to keep life.
